## Story

> Sunday, 15 November, 16:40, the Blitzkurier depot. The city marathon closed the streets all day, and tonight everyone who ran, watched or got stuck orders dinner. A storm is rolling in.
>
> Since the new app went live last week, the delivery-time model can't promise anything for a new order, and Jonas, who built it, is on a boat with no signal. Every order needs a promise before it is accepted, and the first ones come in at 17:00. What dispatch has: two months of raw orders, Jonas's notes and Ilse, the night dispatcher, who knows the city.
>
> Build a model that can promise tonight. This room loads Python with pandas and scikit-learn, so the first puzzle you open takes a little while.

## Stations

### 1. The raw log

**Practises:** Datetime features: pd.to_datetime, .dt.hour and .dt.dayofweek, a rush-hour flag from domain knowledge instead of the raw hour  
**Needs:** 🔎 The shift plan, 🔎 The note by the server  
**Data:** [orders.py](../../content/rooms/ml-courier/data/orders.py)

**Task:**

> The dispatch terminal shows the order log as it was exported: `orders` has one row per order of September and October, indexed by order number, with the minutes from order to door in `minutes`. Its `ordered_at` column is plain text, and Jonas's model only ever read numbers. Does the time of day cost minutes, and how many?
>
> 1. Turn `ordered_at` into timestamps and take the hour and the weekday from them.
> 2. Fit a `LinearRegression` on the items and the hour as a number, and one on the items and a 0/1 column `rush` that marks dispatch's rush hours. Fit each on dispatch's training part, and store their test MAE in minutes as `mae_hour` and `mae_rush`.
> 3. Store what the rush flag adds, in minutes, as `rush_minutes`.

<details><summary>Starter code</summary>

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

print(orders[["ordered_at", "items", "minutes"]].head())
print(orders["ordered_at"].dtype)   # text, not a time

y = orders["minutes"]

mae_hour = None       # test MAE: the items and the hour as a number
mae_rush = None       # test MAE: the items and the rush flag
rush_minutes = None   # what the rush flag adds, in minutes
```

</details>

**Model solution:**

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

y = orders["minutes"]
t = pd.to_datetime(orders["ordered_at"])
hour, weekday = t.dt.hour, t.dt.dayofweek
rush = ((hour.between(12, 13) & (weekday < 5)) | hour.between(17, 19)).astype(int)


def test_mae(X):
    X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=4)
    model = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)
    return mean_absolute_error(y_test, model.predict(X_test)), model


mae_hour, _ = test_mae(pd.DataFrame({"items": orders["items"], "hour": hour}))
mae_rush, model = test_mae(pd.DataFrame({"items": orders["items"], "rush": rush}))
rush_minutes = model.coef_[1]
print(round(mae_hour, 2), round(mae_rush, 2), round(rush_minutes, 1))
```

**Checked result** (`_raw_log_check(mae_hour, mae_rush, rush_minutes)`):

```json
"parsed"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> Rush hour adds **9 minutes** (8.9) to an order. The hour as a number can't show it: a straight line in the hour can only rise or fall all day, but the minutes go up at lunch, down in the afternoon and up again in the evening. A flag built from what dispatch knows about its own city beats the raw number, and on a Sunday the lunch rush simply doesn't happen.

**Hints:**

1. The shift plan on the wall says when dispatch has every courier on the road, and the note by the server says how dispatch tests its models. `pd.to_datetime(orders["ordered_at"])` gives timestamps; `.dt.hour` and `.dt.dayofweek` (Monday = 0) take them apart.
2. `rush = ((hour.between(12, 13) & (weekday < 5)) \| hour.between(17, 19)).astype(int)`. Split once with dispatch's rule, then fit both models on the same training rows.
3. `X = pd.DataFrame({"items": orders["items"], "rush": rush})`, `X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=4)`, `m = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)`, `mae_rush = mean_absolute_error(y_test, m.predict(X_test))`, `rush_minutes = m.coef_[1]`. The same with `hour` instead of `rush` gives `mae_hour`.

### 2. Couriers can't fly

**Practises:** An engineered feature: Euclidean vs Manhattan distance from coordinates, reading a coefficient in other units  
**Needs:** 🔎 The city map, 🔎 The note by the server  
**Data:** [orders.py](../../content/rooms/ml-courier/data/orders.py)

**Task:**

> The map room's terminal still has Jonas's half-finished routing sheet open. `orders` has every pickup and drop-off as grid coordinates (`pickup_x`, `pickup_y`, `drop_x`, `drop_y`). How long does a courier need per block?
>
> 1. Compute the straight-line distance between pickup and drop-off, and the distance a courier really rides.
> 2. Fit a `LinearRegression` on each distance alone, on dispatch's training part, and store their test MAE in minutes as `mae_straight` and `mae_street`.
> 3. Store what one more block adds in the model on the distance a courier rides, in seconds, as `seconds_per_block`.

```python
dx = orders["drop_x"] - orders["pickup_x"]
dy = orders["drop_y"] - orders["pickup_y"]
```

**Model solution:**

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

dx = orders["drop_x"] - orders["pickup_x"]
dy = orders["drop_y"] - orders["pickup_y"]
y = orders["minutes"]


def test_mae(X):
    X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=4)
    model = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)
    return mean_absolute_error(y_test, model.predict(X_test)), model


mae_straight, _ = test_mae(pd.DataFrame({"distance": np.hypot(dx, dy)}))
mae_street, model = test_mae(pd.DataFrame({"blocks": dx.abs() + dy.abs()}))
seconds_per_block = model.coef_[0] * 60
print(round(mae_straight, 2), round(mae_street, 2), round(seconds_per_block))
```

**Checked result** (`_street_check(mae_straight, mae_street, seconds_per_block)`):

```json
"routed"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> A courier needs **85 seconds per block**. The straight line is shorter than any real route, and by how much depends on the direction: a trip straight along one street is as long as the crow flies, a diagonal one up to 41 % longer. The street distance, `abs(dx) + abs(dy)`, is what the bike actually rides, and alone it already beats the straight line. A feature that matches how the world works is worth more than any model tuning.

**Hints:**

1. Look at the city map on the wall: how do the streets run? The split follows the note by the server. `np.hypot(dx, dy)` is the straight line.
2. With no diagonal streets, a courier rides all of `dx` along one street and all of `dy` along another: `dx.abs() + dy.abs()` blocks. Fit each distance as a one-column table, e.g. `pd.DataFrame({"blocks": blocks})`.
3. `X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(pd.DataFrame({"blocks": blocks}), orders["minutes"], test_size=0.25, random_state=4)`, `m = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)`, `mae_street = mean_absolute_error(y_test, m.predict(X_test))`, `seconds_per_block = m.coef_[0] * 60`. The same with `np.hypot(dx, dy)` gives `mae_straight`.

### 3. Weather and vehicles

**Practises:** Encoding categories: OneHotEncoder for unordered ones, OrdinalEncoder with an explicit order, a ColumnTransformer in a pipeline, a category the training data has never seen  
**Needs:** 🔎 The weather service's poster  
**Data:** [orders.py](../../content/rooms/ml-courier/data/orders.py)

**Task:**

> At the radio desk, the trainee has started a model that reads the vehicle (`bike`, `scooter`, `cargo`) and the weather as words. Tonight a storm is coming. How many minutes does a storm add over a dry evening?
>
> 1. Fix the trainee's pipeline: the vehicle one-hot encoded, the weather turned into its level, the items kept, then a `LinearRegression`, fitted on all orders. Keep it as `model`.
> 2. Store how many minutes your model adds for a storm instead of dry weather, everything else equal, as `storm_minutes`.

**Model solution:**

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, OrdinalEncoder

encode = ColumnTransformer([
    ("vehicle", OneHotEncoder(), ["vehicle"]),
    ("weather", OrdinalEncoder(categories=[["dry", "drizzle", "rain", "storm"]]), ["weather"]),
], remainder="passthrough")
model = make_pipeline(encode, LinearRegression())
model.fit(orders[["vehicle", "weather", "items"]], orders["minutes"])

evening = pd.DataFrame({"vehicle": ["bike", "bike"], "weather": ["dry", "storm"], "items": [3, 3]})
p = model.predict(evening)
storm_minutes = p[1] - p[0]
print(p.round(1), round(storm_minutes, 1))
```

**Checked result** (`_weather_check(model, storm_minutes)`):

```json
"forecast"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> A storm adds **12 minutes** (11.9) over a dry evening: about 4 minutes per level. The log has never seen a storm, so no encoder can learn one from it. One-hot encoding either refuses the unknown word or, with `handle_unknown="ignore"`, quietly prices a storm like a dry night. The service's scale puts the weather in order, and a level on that scale lets a linear model carry on past the last level it has seen. The default `OrdinalEncoder` sorts words alphabetically, which puts drizzle before dry.

**Hints:**

1. The weather service's poster by the radio shows its scale. Run the starter: what does the encoder say about `'storm'`? And print `encode.named_transformers_["weather"].categories_` to see the order it chose.
2. `OrdinalEncoder(categories=[["dry", "drizzle", "rain", "storm"]])` turns the words into 0 to 3, in that order, and knows a storm even though the log has none.
3. With that encoder in the `ColumnTransformer`, fit again, then `p = model.predict(evening)` and `storm_minutes = p[1] - p[0]`.

### 4. Too good to be true

**Practises:** Data leakage: columns known only after the target, a suspiciously good score, an honest test MAE, a business metric from the predictions  
**Needs:** 1. The raw log (its result), 3. Weather and vehicles (its result), 🔒 1. The raw log, 🔎 The data dictionary, 🔎 The Blitzkurier poster, 🔎 The note by the server  
**Data:** [orders.py](../../content/rooms/ml-courier/data/orders.py)

**Code lock** (opens with `912`):

> Jonas's laptop is locked. On a sticky note under the keyboard: "PIN = what rush hour adds, then what a storm adds, both in whole minutes."

**Task:**

> Jonas's laptop holds the model that promised every delivery until the new app went live last week. On his test part it scores an R² of almost 1. Since the switch, it can't promise anything for a new order. Is it as good as it looks?
>
> 1. Run Jonas's code. Find every column that dispatch doesn't know yet when an order comes in, and store their names as `leaks`.
> 2. Fit the same model on the remaining number columns, on dispatch's split, and store its test MAE in minutes as `honest_mae`.
> 3. Store how many of the test orders the honest model would have had to refund as `refunds`.

<details><summary>Starter code</summary>

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, r2_score
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# Jonas's model: every number column of the log
y = orders["minutes"]
numbers = orders.select_dtypes("number").drop(columns="minutes")
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(numbers, y)
jonas = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)
print("R²", r2_score(y_test, jonas.predict(X_test)))
print("MAE", mean_absolute_error(y_test, jonas.predict(X_test)))
```

**Model solution:**

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

y = orders["minutes"]
numbers = orders.select_dtypes("number").drop(columns="minutes")
leaks = ["kitchen_wait", "gps_pings", "rating"]
honest = numbers.drop(columns=leaks)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(honest, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=4)
model = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)
p = model.predict(X_test)
honest_mae = mean_absolute_error(y_test, p)
refunds = int(((y_test - p) > 10).sum())
print(round(honest_mae, 2), refunds)
```

**Checked result** (`_leak_check(leaks, honest_mae, refunds)`):

```json
"sealed"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> Without `kitchen_wait`, `gps_pings` and `rating`, Jonas's model misses by 5.8 minutes, not 0.6, and **48** of the 500 test orders would have been free. The GPS pings count the minutes on the road, the kitchen wait is only known at pickup, and the stars come after the door: each was known only once the answer was. That is data leakage. A test score is only honest if the model sees exactly what it will see when it is used, and for a new order the app has none of these yet.

**Hints:**

1. The data dictionary next to the laptop says when each column is filled in. The poster on the wall says when a delivery is free. And Jonas's split doesn't follow the note by the server yet.
2. Anything filled in after the order (at pickup, on the road, after the door) is a leak. `numbers.drop(columns=leaks)`, then the split with `test_size=0.25, random_state=4`. A refund is a test order that took more than 10 minutes longer than the model promised: `(y_test - prediction) > 10`.
3. `leaks = ["kitchen_wait", "gps_pings", "rating"]`, `honest = numbers.drop(columns=leaks)`, split, fit, `p = model.predict(X_test)`, `honest_mae = mean_absolute_error(y_test, p)`, `refunds = int(((y_test - p) > 10).sum())`.

**Task:**

> Every courier box sends 40 telemetry channels when an order is dispatched, `s01` to `s40` in `orders`. Ilse has already run a filter over them at the telemetry rack. Which channels should dispatch stream tonight?
>
> 1. Run Ilse's filter and look at the channels it ranks highest.
> 2. Start from a `LinearRegression` on the distance a courier rides and the items, and find the channels that lower its test MAE most on dispatch's split. Store their numbers as a list, `channels`.
> 3. Store the test MAE of the distance, the items and your channels as `mae_best`.

**Model solution:**

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

telemetry = orders[[f"s{i:02d}" for i in range(1, 41)]]
y = orders["minutes"]
blocks = (orders["drop_x"] - orders["pickup_x"]).abs() + (orders["drop_y"] - orders["pickup_y"]).abs()
base = pd.DataFrame({"blocks": blocks, "items": orders["items"]})


def test_mae(X):
    X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=4)
    model = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)
    return mean_absolute_error(y_test, model.predict(X_test))


maes = {c: test_mae(base.assign(**{c: orders[c]})) for c in telemetry.columns}
best = sorted(maes, key=maes.get)[:2]
print(best, [round(maes[c], 2) for c in best], "channel 9:", round(maes["s09"], 2))
channels = sorted(int(c[1:]) for c in best)
mae_best = test_mae(base.assign(**{c: orders[c] for c in best}))
print(channels, round(mae_best, 2))
```

**Checked result** (`_channels_check(channels, mae_best)`):

```json
"tuned"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> Dispatch streams channels **14** (the battery) and **31** (the load). Ilse's filter ranks channel 9 near the top because it goes well with the minutes, but it is the nav unit's planned route length: the street distance again, with noise. Next to the distance it adds nothing, and it would take one of the two places. A filter scores each column alone; to know what a column adds to the ones you have, test it inside the model, by adding it (forward selection), by taking it away, or with `permutation_importance`.

**Hints:**

1. The fax by the dispatch console says how many channels come through tonight, and the manual on the rack says what some channels measure. Look up channel 9 there.
2. Loop over the 40 channels: add each one to the table of street distance and items, fit, and note the test MAE. The two lowest win. `SequentialFeatureSelector` does the same, but it may also drop the distance.
3. `base = pd.DataFrame({"blocks": blocks, "items": orders["items"]})`; for each `c` in `telemetry.columns`, split `base.assign(**{c: orders[c]})` with `test_size=0.25, random_state=4`, fit and store the MAE in a dict; `sorted(maes, key=maes.get)[:2]` gives `s14` and `s31`. Then the same with both for `mae_best`.

**Task:**

The manager will only switch a model on if dispatch can feed it raw orders as they arrive, and if it misses old orders it has never seen by less than 2.4 minutes on average. What does Blitzkurier promise tonight?
>
> 1. Build one pipeline that takes raw order rows, the columns of `tonight`, turns them into everything you learned tonight and ends in a regressor. A `FunctionTransformer` runs your own function as a step. Fit it on the log and keep it as `model`.
> 2. Store its promises for tonight's eight orders, in whole minutes, as `promises`.

**Model solution:**

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import FunctionTransformer, OneHotEncoder, OrdinalEncoder


def features(df):
    """Raw order rows in, model features out."""
    t = pd.to_datetime(df["ordered_at"])
    hour, weekday = t.dt.hour, t.dt.dayofweek
    out = pd.DataFrame(index=df.index)
    out["rush"] = ((hour.between(12, 13) & (weekday < 5)) | hour.between(17, 19)).astype(int)
    out["blocks"] = (df["drop_x"] - df["pickup_x"]).abs() + (df["drop_y"] - df["pickup_y"]).abs()
    for c in ["items", "vehicle", "weather", "s14", "s31"]:
        out[c] = df[c]
    return out


encode = ColumnTransformer([
    ("vehicle", OneHotEncoder(), ["vehicle"]),
    ("weather", OrdinalEncoder(categories=[["dry", "drizzle", "rain", "storm"]]), ["weather"]),
], remainder="passthrough")
model = make_pipeline(FunctionTransformer(features), encode, LinearRegression())
model.fit(orders.drop(columns="minutes"), orders["minutes"])

promises = model.predict(tonight).round()
print(pd.Series(promises, index=tonight.index))
```

**Checked result** (`_promises_check(model, promises)`):

```json
"promised"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> The console goes green at 17:02. The first promise goes out: 40 minutes for order 52001, a bike in the storm with the evening rush. On orders it has never seen, your pipeline misses by about 2.2 minutes, and it reads nothing the app doesn't have yet.
>
> Every step went into it: the rush flag from a text column, the street distance from four coordinates, the storm on the weather service's scale, the leaks left out, and two channels chosen inside the model. The model itself is a plain linear regression. Its features do the work.

**Hints:**

1. Go through the room's other stations: each one found a feature, an encoding or a column to leave out. The fax by this console says how many channels come through tonight.
2. In `features(df)`, build `rush` from `ordered_at`, `blocks` from the coordinates, and keep `items`, `vehicle`, `weather`, `s14` and `s31`. Then a `ColumnTransformer` with `OneHotEncoder()` on `vehicle`, `OrdinalEncoder` with the service's scale on `weather`, and `remainder="passthrough"`.
3. `model = make_pipeline(FunctionTransformer(features), encode, LinearRegression())`, `model.fit(orders.drop(columns="minutes"), orders["minutes"])`, `promises = model.predict(tonight).round()`.

## Clues in the room

### 🔎 The shift plan

*Used by: 1. The raw log*

> A laminated sheet on the dispatch wall, coffee rings on it.
>
> **SHIFT PLAN, AUTUMN**
> **Lunch rush**, Monday to Friday, 12:00 to 13:59: every courier on the road.
> **Evening rush**, every day, 17:00 to 19:59: every courier on the road.
> All other hours: half the fleet, the rest on call.
>
> Scribbled underneath: "Weekends the offices are shut, nobody orders lunch to their desk. — Ilse"

### 🔎 The note by the server

*Used by: 1. The raw log, 2. Couriers can't fly, 4. Too good to be true, 5. Forty sensors*

> Taped to the server cabinet, in Jonas's handwriting:
>
> "Every model gets tested the same way, so we can compare: a quarter of the orders held back, `test_size=0.25`, and `random_state=4`, our depot number. Scores on the training rows don't count."

### 🔎 The city map

*Used by: 2. Couriers can't fly*

> A huge map of the city covers the wall, drawn as a grid: 31 streets run north to south, numbered 0 to 30 along the bottom edge (x), and 31 run west to east, numbered 0 to 30 up the side (y). Between them, block after block of houses, yards and parks. Not one street runs diagonally.
>
> A courier's sticker in the corner: "Couriers can't fly."

### 🔎 The weather service's poster

*Used by: 3. Weather and vehicles*

> A poster from the city's weather service, pinned above the radio:
>
> **WEATHER WARNING LEVELS FOR ROAD TRAFFIC**
> 0 dry
> 1 drizzle
> 2 rain
> 3 storm
>
> In red marker, across the bottom: "Sunday 15 Nov, from 16:00: level 3."

### 🔎 The data dictionary

*Used by: 4. Too good to be true*

> A stapled printout next to Jonas's laptop: what each column of the order log means, and when the app fills it in.
>
> `ordered_at`: when the order was placed. Filled in at the order.
> `pickup_x`, `pickup_y`, `drop_x`, `drop_y`: restaurant and door on the city grid. At the order.
> `weather`: the weather service's level. At the order.
> `vehicle`: the courier dispatch assigns. At the order.
> `items`: dishes in the bag. At the order.
> `kitchen_wait`: minutes the courier waited at the restaurant. When the courier picks up.
> `gps_pings`: one ping per minute on the road. During the ride.
> `rating`: the customer's stars. After the delivery.
> `s01` to `s40`: the courier box's telemetry. At the order, when dispatch assigns the courier.
> `minutes`: order to door. At the door.

### 🔎 The Blitzkurier poster

*Used by: 4. Too good to be true*

> A bright orange poster, the same one that hangs in every tram in the city:
>
> **BLITZKURIER. WE PROMISE, WE DELIVER.**
> More than 10 minutes later than we promised? Your order is on us.

### 🔎 The fax from the network operator

*Used by: 5. Forty sensors, 6. Tonight's promises*

> A fax, still curled, in the tray next to the dispatch console:
>
> "To all fleet customers. Marathon day: the mobile network along the course is overloaded from 16:00 until midnight. Each vehicle box can stream **two** telemetry channels to your server during that time. Please tell us which two before 17:00. — CityNet Operations"

### 🔎 The courier box manual

*Used by: 5. Forty sensors*

> A greasy manual hanging on a chain from the rack, open at "Telemetry channels":
>
> `s02` cabin temperature
> `s09` nav unit: planned route length
> `s14` battery charge
> `s17` tyre pressure
> `s22` signal strength
> `s31` load sensor
> `s38` GPS satellites in view
> All other channels: internal diagnostics.

## Handbook in the room: 📖 The dispatch wiki

**Dates and times:** [`pd.to_datetime(s)`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.to_datetime.html), [`s.dt.hour  s.dt.dayofweek`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.dt.dayofweek.html), [`s.between(a, b)  s.isin([...])`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.between.html)

**Distances:** [`np.hypot(dx, dy)`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.hypot.html), [`s.abs()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.abs.html)

**Encoding categories:** [`OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown=…)`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.preprocessing.OneHotEncoder.html), [`OrdinalEncoder(categories=[[…]])`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.preprocessing.OrdinalEncoder.html), [`ColumnTransformer([(name, transformer, columns), …], remainder=…)`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.compose.ColumnTransformer.html)

**Pipelines:** [`make_pipeline(step, …, model)`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.pipeline.make_pipeline.html), [`FunctionTransformer(func)`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.preprocessing.FunctionTransformer.html)

**Leakage:** [`Data leakage`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html#data-leakage), [`df.select_dtypes("number")`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.select_dtypes.html)

**Choosing features:** [`SelectKBest(f_regression, k=…)`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.feature_selection.SelectKBest.html), [`SequentialFeatureSelector(model, n_features_to_select=…)`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.feature_selection.SequentialFeatureSelector.html), [`permutation_importance(model, X, y)`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.inspection.permutation_importance.html), [`df.assign(name=values)`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.assign.html)
